items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data
items.why: The binding UK rule on timing: before the processing. Article 35(7)(c) requires 'an assessment of the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects', which is wider than privacy. Amended 30 September 2026 only to substitute 'Commission' in paragraphs 4 and 5; no known outstanding effects.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: What is a DPIA?
items.locator: Section 'What kind of ‘risk’ do they assess?'
items.quote: This includes risks to privacy and data protection rights, but also effects on other fundamental rights and interests.
items.why: Source of the quotation. The regulator's reading that the UK assessment already reaches discrimination, economic or social disadvantage and, in some cases, the impact on society. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed; page metadata gives 9 October 2025.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.locator: Section 'What do we need to consider when undertaking data protection impact assessments for AI?', paragraph beginning 'In addition to conducting a DPIA'
items.quote: public sector organisations are required to undertake equality impact assessments
items.why: How the regulator sees the two kinds of assessment sitting together: other impact assessments may be required or done voluntarily alongside the data protection one. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed; page metadata gives 11 December 2024.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 149: Public sector equality duty
items.quote: A public authority must, in the exercise of its functions, have due regard to the need to
items.why: The nearest UK statutory counterpart to a rights assessment for public bodies. A duty to have due regard, not a duty to produce a document; the statute does not use the words 'equality impact assessment'. Applies to public authorities and those exercising public functions.

items.title: Human Rights Act 1998, section 6: Acts of public authorities
items.quote: It is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way which is incompatible with a Convention right.
items.why: Why fundamental rights matter to UK public bodies using AI whether or not any assessment is prescribed. Creates no assessment duty.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: Prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2)
items.why: The EU's fundamental rights assessment. Who: bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III point 5(b) and (c) systems (credit scoring; life and health insurance risk and pricing); critical infrastructure is excluded. What: the six elements in paragraph 1, including affected groups, specific harms, human oversight and complaint mechanisms. Results notified to the market surveillance authority. Paragraph 4 allows cross-reference to the data protection assessment. Article 99(4) does not list Article 27 among the provisions carrying the EUR 15 000 000 fine. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Recital 96
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: After performing that impact assessment, the deployer should notify the relevant market surveillance authority.
items.why: Explains the purpose of the assessment and suggests involving representatives of affected groups, independent experts and civil society. A recital, so an aid to interpretation, not a rule. Names banking or insurance entities as examples of the deployers covered and mentions complaint handling and redress; the word 'dignity' does not appear. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: deployers of high-risk AI systems shall use the information provided under Article 13 of this Regulation to comply with their obligation
items.why: The link running the other way: the provider's information must be used to carry out the data protection impact assessment. With Article 27(4) this is the textual basis for treating the two assessments as one joined exercise. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 111: AI systems already placed on the market or put into service
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: shall take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation by 2 August 2030
items.why: Source of the figure. High-risk systems on the market or in service before Chapter III applies are covered only if their design then changes significantly, but providers and deployers of systems intended to be used by public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030. Article 113(c)(i), read alongside, dates the Annex III high-risk rules, Article 27 among them, from 2 December 2027. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: This section should provide information on impact assessments conducted, identified risks, and mitigation efforts.
items.why: UK public sector practice on publishing assessments, which bears on the top level of the question. Page shows 'Updated 8 May 2025'. Public sector only; names no fundamental rights assessment.

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division); The National Archives, Find Case Law
items.locator: Paragraphs 152-154 (data protection impact assessment); paragraphs 199-201 (public sector equality duty)
items.quote: the DPIA failed properly to assess the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
items.why: The leading UK judgment on both halves of the question. The force had written an impact assessment for live facial recognition, and the court still held it inadequate because it did not grapple with the rights engaged; it also held that the force had 'not done all that they reasonably could' to meet the equality duty, never having checked the software for race or sex bias. Decided under section 64 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (law enforcement processing), not Article 35, and concerns a police force.

items.title: Chelmer Valley High School (reprimand)
items.quote: The school failed to complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) prior to introducing facial recognition technology for the purposes of cashless catering.
items.why: Regulator enforcement on timing: a reprimand under Article 35(1) for putting a biometric system into use with no prior assessment. A reprimand, not a fine, against a school; only the regulator's summary page was read, not the reprimand document.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
items.locator: Section 'What does the ICO consider likely to result in high risk?', item 'Innovative technology'; section 'What does 'innovative technologies' mean?'
items.quote: processing involving the use of innovative technologies, or the novel application of existing technologies (including AI)
items.why: The screening rule behind the middle level of the question: the regulator's Art. 35(4) list names AI as innovative technology, and an assessment is required when that is combined with another listed factor such as evaluation or scoring. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed on the page; the year given is the year it was read.

items.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology; Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation; Cabinet Office; Office for Artificial Intelligence
items.locator: Point 2 'Deliver fair services for all of our users and citizens', practical steps; point 1 'Test to avoid any unintended outcomes or consequences'
items.quote: You must do an Equality Impact Assessment to adhere to the Equality Act (2010) and Public Sector Equality Duty
items.why: Government's own instruction to departments to run the equality and data protection assessments together and regularly. It goes further than the statute, which requires due regard and does not name an assessment document. Guidance for government departments only; last updated 2023.

items.title: Introduction to AI assurance
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 4 'The AI assurance toolkit', list of assurance mechanisms
items.quote: Used to anticipate the wider effects of a system/product on the environment, equality, human rights, data protection, or other outcomes.
items.why: Places the impact assessment among assurance mechanisms, alongside audit and conformity assessment by third parties, which bears on the top level of the question (assessments independently assured). Introductory guidance with no legal force.

items.title: A systematic review of artificial intelligence impact assessments
items.publisher: Artificial Intelligence Review (Springer Nature); B. C. Stahl and others
items.quote: Working with a population of 181 documents, the authors identified 38 actual AI-IAs and subjected them to a rigorous qualitative analysis
items.why: Peer-reviewed systematic review, open access, led from a UK university. Finds some convergence in what AI impact assessments cover but warns of fragmentation and of grading that is open to interpretation, which is the case for one joined template. Literature search ran January to June 2021, so it pre-dates the AI Act's fundamental rights assessment.

items.title: An Institutional View of Algorithmic Impact Assessments
items.publisher: Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, Volume 35, Number 1; A. D. Selbst
items.locator: Abstract; body text on documentation and discrimination law (passage before footnote 100)
items.quote: The ex ante documentation requirement enables the possibility of an ex post remedy.
items.why: Explains why an assessment done before deployment matters to the people affected: it creates the record that later lets a harm be proved and put right. Also argues that a regime relying on firms' own discretion can be undermined by their incentives. United States law review article, edited by students and not peer reviewed in the journal sense; written about US law.

items.title: Algorithmic impact assessment: a case study in healthcare
items.quote: AIAs are currently largely untested in public-sector contexts.
items.why: UK evidence: a worked proposal for an impact assessment, with public participation and publication, as a condition of access to NHS imaging data. Useful for the levels that ask about consultation and publishing. A proposal for one programme, published by a research institute and not peer reviewed; dated 2022.

items.title: NSW AI Assessment Framework
items.locator: Sections 'What is it?' and 'When should it be used?'
items.quote: reassessed when there are significant changes to their features, datasets, purpose or decision-making contexts
items.why: International comparator: a mandatory assessment covering fairness, privacy, transparency and accountability together, started early and repeated on change, for AI that is bought as well as built. New South Wales public sector only, under Circular DCS-2026-02; a self-assessment, with independent review only for high and critical risk. No date printed on the page.
